learn: The components of an effective prompt
Automatic prompt engineering and prompt chaining
intro.why: Prompting is the cheapest and fastest way to adapt a model: no training, instant iteration. Production systems depend on prompts that are reliable, testable and produce machine-readable output.

sections.title: Prompt components
sections.plain: A good prompt says who the model is, what to do, with what information, shown by examples, in what format.
sections.body:
Effective prompts usually combine:

  • Role / persona: "You are a careful support assistant." Sets tone and expertise.
  • Instruction: the task, stated clearly and early.
  • Context: the information needed (documents, definitions, constraints), separated by delimiters.
  • Examples: input–output demonstrations.
  • Output format: exact shape of the answer (one word, a list, JSON with given keys).

Code example ex1 assembles all five into a ticket-classification prompt. Missing pieces force the model to guess: without a format it may explain instead of labelling; without examples, label boundaries are fuzzy. Prompts should be versioned and tested against example sets like any other code.

sections.title: Zero-shot, few-shot and in-context learning
sections.plain: Either just describe the task, or also show a few solved examples in the prompt, and the model picks up the pattern.
sections.body:
Zero-shot: instruction only. One-/few-shot: include k solved examples. In-context learning (ICL) is the ability to infer the task from those examples without any weight update, an emergent property of large pre-trained models.

Practical findings: examples should be representative and label-balanced (imbalance biases predictions toward the majority label); order matters (recent examples weigh more); the format and label space shown matter as much as exact correctness; gains diminish as k grows while token cost rises linearly. Instruction-tuned models often do well zero-shot, so try that first and add examples where they reduce errors.

sections.title: Instruction prompting
sections.plain: Be specific: say who the answer is for, how long, what tone, and what a good answer contains.
sections.body:
Instructions work best when they remove guesswork:

  • State audience, length, tone and constraints: "Explain inflation to a 12-year-old in 3 short sentences, friendly tone, no jargon, with one everyday price example."
  • Put instructions before the data and wrap data in delimiters, so text inside the data isn't mistaken for instructions (important for prompt-injection resistance, M15).
  • Say what to do, not only what to avoid.
  • Give the model a way out: "If the answer is not in the context, say you don't know."
  • Break complex tasks into numbered steps.

sections.title: Self-consistency
sections.plain: Ask several times with some randomness and go with the most common answer.
sections.body:
Self-consistency samples n reasoning paths at temperature > 0 and returns the most frequent final answer. If samples are independent and each is correct with probability p > 0.5, majority accuracy rises with n:

$$P(\text{majority correct}) = \sum_{k>n/2} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$

Worked (ex1): p = 0.6 → n = 5: 0.68, n = 21: 0.83; p = 0.7 → n = 21: 0.97. Answers 42, 42, 7, 42 → 42. In practice wrong answers are spread over many values, so the correct one wins even more often, but correlated errors limit gains. Cost scales with n. It is most useful for tasks with a single checkable final answer (maths, classification); M11 combines it with chain-of-thought.

sections.title: Automatic prompt engineering and chaining
sections.plain: Let a model write and test candidate prompts; and split big tasks into a chain of smaller prompts.
sections.body:
Automatic prompt engineering (APE) treats the instruction as something to search for: an LLM proposes candidate instructions from input–output examples, each is scored on a validation set, and the best (or refined variants) are kept. Related tools optimise prompts or few-shot selections programmatically.

Prompt chaining decomposes a task into steps, each a separate prompt whose output feeds the next. In ex2: extract facts (4) → keep numeric facts (3) → write a summary. Benefits: simpler prompts, inspectable intermediate results, per-step validation and different models per step. Costs: more calls, latency and the chance that an early error propagates.

sections.title: Function calling
sections.plain: Give the model a menu of tools; it replies with a structured request, your code runs the tool, and the model uses the result.
sections.body:
With function calling (tool use), the prompt describes available functions: name, description and a JSON schema for arguments. The model decides when a tool is needed and emits a structured call such as {"tool": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune", "unit": "C"}}. The application validates the arguments, executes the function, and returns the result in a new message; the model then writes the final answer.

Good practice: clear tool descriptions, strict schema validation (ex2 rejects a call missing "unit" and asks for a retry), permission checks before side-effecting actions, timeouts, and treating tool outputs as untrusted data. Function calling is the foundation of agents (M13).

sections.title: Structured output and constrained decoding
sections.plain: Force the model's output to follow a format by blocking any token that would break it.
sections.body:
Downstream code needs parseable output. Options, from weakest to strongest: ask for JSON and show an example; use a provider's JSON or structured-output mode; validate and retry; or use constrained decoding.

Constrained decoding converts a schema, regular expression or grammar into a state machine; at each step tokens that cannot lead to a valid string get probability zero:

$$P'(t) \propto P(t)\cdot m_t,\quad m_t\in\{0,1\}$$

Worked (ex2): after "age": the unconstrained top token is "forty" (0.32); masking all non-integer tokens makes "42" certain. The output is guaranteed to parse, but constraints ensure form, not truth, and overly tight constraints can hurt reasoning quality (let the model think first, then format).

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Prompt sensitivity: small wording or example-order changes can shift accuracy; evaluate on a test set, not one example.
  • System vs user messages: system prompts set persistent behaviour; user content should be treated as data where possible.
  • Long prompts cost: tokens add latency and money (M6); prefix caching helps repeated instructions.
  • Prompts are model-specific: re-test when switching models.

code.title: Prompt assembly and self-consistency maths
code.explain: Builds a few-shot classification prompt from role, instruction, context, two examples and an output format, then computes majority-vote accuracy for p = 0.6 and 0.7 with n = 1–21 samples (e.g. 0.6 → 0.83 at n = 21) and votes over sampled answers 42, 42, 7, 42.
mistakes: Expecting voting to help when p < 0.5.
code.code:
"""Assembling a prompt from components, few-shot formatting, and why self-consistency (majority voting) helps."""
from math import comb

def build_prompt(role, instruction, context, examples, output_format, query):
    parts = [f"System: {role}", f"Instruction: {instruction}"]
    if context: parts.append(f"Context: {context}")
    for x, y in examples: parts.append(f"Input: {x}\nOutput: {y}")
    parts.append(f"Output format: {output_format}")
    parts.append(f"Input: {query}\nOutput:")
    return "\n".join(parts)

p = build_prompt(
    role="You are a careful support assistant.",
    instruction="Classify the ticket as billing, technical or account.",
    context="Billing covers invoices and refunds.",
    examples=[("I was charged twice", "billing"), ("App crashes on login", "technical")],
    output_format="one lowercase word",
    query="Please change my registered email")
print(p)
print(f"--- zero-shot uses 0 examples; this few-shot prompt uses 2; length {len(p.split())} words")

# Self-consistency: sample n reasoning paths, take the majority answer.
def majority_correct(p, n):
    """Probability that more than half of n independent samples are correct (binary simplification)."""
    return sum(comb(n, k) * p**k * (1-p)**(n-k) for k in range(n//2 + 1, n + 1))
for p_single in (0.6, 0.7):
    print(f"single-sample accuracy {p_single}: " + ", ".join(f"n={n}: {majority_correct(p_single, n):.3f}" for n in (1, 5, 11, 21)))
votes = [42, 42, 7, 42]
best = max(set(votes), key=votes.count)
print(f"sampled answers {votes} -> majority {best} ({votes.count(best)}/{len(votes)})")
print("voting helps only when individual samples are right more often than any single wrong answer")
code.output:

code.title: Tool calls, chaining and constrained decoding
code.explain: Parses and validates a JSON tool call, executes it and returns the result, rejects a call with a missing argument, runs a three-step extract → filter → summarise chain, and masks invalid tokens so that "42" replaces "forty" after "age":.
mistakes: Trusting JSON mode to make content correct.
code.notes: A stub function stands in for a real weather API.
code.code:
"""Function calling with schema validation, prompt chaining, and constrained decoding with a token mask."""
import json, math

tools = {"get_weather": {"params": {"city": str, "unit": str}, "fn": lambda city, unit: {"city": city, "temp": 21 if unit == "C" else 70, "unit": unit}}}
model_output = '{"tool": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune", "unit": "C"}}'
call = json.loads(model_output)
spec = tools[call["tool"]]
ok = all(k in call["arguments"] and isinstance(call["arguments"][k], t) for k, t in spec["params"].items())
print("model emitted:", model_output)
print("schema valid:", ok)
result = spec["fn"](**call["arguments"])
print("tool result fed back to the model:", json.dumps(result))
print("final answer the model can now write: It is 21 degrees C in Pune.")

bad = '{"tool": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune"}}'
args = json.loads(bad)["arguments"]
missing = [k for k in spec["params"] if k not in args]
print("invalid call missing:", missing, "-> ask the model to retry with an error message")

# Prompt chaining: each step's output becomes the next step's input
doc = "Revenue rose 12% to 3.4 billion. Costs rose 20%. Margin fell to 18%. The team thanked customers."
step1 = [s.strip() for s in doc.rstrip(".").split(". ") if s.strip()]           # extract facts
step2 = [s for s in step1 if "%" in s]                              # keep quantitative facts
step3 = "Summary: " + "; ".join(step2)                             # write summary
print("chain:", len(step1), "facts ->", len(step2), "numeric facts ->", step3)

# Constrained decoding: allow only tokens that keep the output valid
vocab = ["{", "}", "\"age\"", ":", "42", "forty", "\"name\"", "hello"]
logits = [0.1, 0.2, 1.0, 0.3, 1.2, 2.0, 0.4, 1.5]
def softmax(z): m = max(z); e = [math.exp(v - m) for v in z]; s = sum(e); return [v / s for v in e]
allowed_after_colon = {"42"}                                         # grammar: an integer must follow "age":
p = softmax(logits)
print("unconstrained top token:", vocab[p.index(max(p))], f"({max(p):.2f})")
masked = [l if v in allowed_after_colon else -1e9 for v, l in zip(vocab, logits)]
q = softmax(masked)
print("constrained top token  :", vocab[q.index(max(q))], f"({max(q):.2f})  <- invalid tokens masked to zero probability")
